1.q: וַ⁠יֵּשְׁב֖וּ שָׁלֹ֣שׁ שָׁנִ֑ים אֵ֚ין מִלְחָמָ֔ה בֵּ֥ין אֲרָ֖ם וּ⁠בֵ֥ין יִשְׂרָאֵֽל
1.note: The pronoun **they** refers to the kingdoms of **Aram** and **Israel**. It may be more natural in your language to use their names at the beginning of the sentence and a pronoun at the end. Alternate translation: [And Aram and Israel continued three years without war between them]

2.note: The author is using the phrase **And it happened** to introduce a new event in the story. Use a word, phrase, or other method in your language that is natural for introducing a new event.

If your language would not represent a number in a form such as **third**, you could represent this number in a form that your language would use. Alternate translation: [in year three] or [after those three years]
See how you translated the similar expression in 1:25. Alternate translation: [that Jehoshaphat, the king of Judah, went]

3.q: הַ⁠יְדַעְתֶּ֕ם כִּֽי־לָ֖⁠נוּ רָמֹ֣ת גִּלְעָ֑ד וַ⁠אֲנַ֣חְנוּ מַחְשִׁ֔ים מִ⁠קַּ֣חַת אֹתָ֔⁠הּ מִ⁠יַּ֖ד מֶ֥לֶךְ אֲרָֽם
3.note: Ahab is using the question form for emphasis. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [Since Ramoth Gilead rightfully belongs to us, we should not be silent from taking it from the hand of the king of Aram!]

Ahab is speaking as if the Israelites were actually **being silent**. He means that they are doing nothing. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. If you have already translated the book of Judges, see how you translated the similar expression in Judges 18:9. Alternate translation: [but we are doing nothing to take it]

Here, **hand** represents a person’s possession of something. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [from the possession of]

4.note: Ahab is using one Judean who would be involved, Jehoshaphat, addressing him as **you**, to mean all the Judeans who would be involved. He is also using one Israelite who would be involved, himself, to mean all the Israelites who would be involved. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression from your culture or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Will your army go with my army]

4.q: כָּמ֧וֹ⁠נִי כָמ֛וֹ⁠ךָ כְּ⁠עַמִּ֥⁠י כְ⁠עַמֶּ֖⁠ךָ כְּ⁠סוּסַ֥⁠י כְּ⁠סוּסֶֽי⁠ךָ
4.note: Jehoshaphat is using a common expression of his culture to agree to join Ahab in an attack on Ramoth Gilead. If this expression does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I and my army with its horses will fight alongside you and your army with its horses]
In this context, the word **people** means “soldiers.” It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [Like my soldiers, like your soldiers]

5.note: Jehoshaphat is using **as today** as a common expression of his culture to mean “first” or “right now.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [first]

Jehoshaphat is using the **word** of Yahweh to represent what Yahweh would say by using word. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [guidance from Yahweh]

6.note: These prophets are referring to Yahweh by a title rather than by a name. (Jehoshaphat recognizes this, and that is why he asks in the next verse to inquire of a “prophet of Yahweh.”) Some translations, following traditional Jewish usage, represent the divine name Yahweh as “the Lord,” often using small caps or all caps to indicate what they are doing. If you have chosen to do that in your translation, be sure not to use caps here. That way it will be clear that these prophets are not speaking in the name of Yahweh. (Another way to make this clear would be to use the term “God,” as the UST does.)
See how you translated the similar expression in 22:3. Alternate translation: [into the possession of the king]

Even though the prophets are addressing the king of Israel directly, they are speaking of him in the third person as **the king** to show respect. If it would be helpful in your language, you could translate this in a respectful form in the second person. Alternate translation: [into your hand, O king] or [into your possession, O king]

7.note: Jehoshaphat is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [that we may seek a message from Yahweh from him]

8.q: וַ⁠אֲנִ֣י שְׂנֵאתִ֗י⁠ו כִּ֠י לֹֽא־יִתְנַבֵּ֨א עָלַ֥⁠י טוֹב֙ כִּ֣י אִם־רָ֔ע
8.note: If it would be more natural in your language, you could reverse the order of these phrases, since the second phrase gives the reason for the result that the first phrase describes. Alternate translation: [but because he does not prophesy good about me but rather evil, I, I hate him]
If your language does not use abstract nouns for the ideas of **good** and **evil**, you could express the same ideas in other ways. Alternate translation: [good things … bad things]
See how you translated the similar expression in 1:17. Alternate translation: [but, personally, I hate him]

Even though Jehoshaphat is addressing Ahab directly, he is speaking of him in the third person as **the king** to show respect. If it would be helpful in your language, you could translate this in a respectful form in the second person. Alternate translation: [May you not say thus, O king]

The author is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [but rather he prophesies evil about me]

Jehoshaphat is politely and tactfully disagreeing with Ahab and suggesting that Micaiah will not necessarily prophesy something evil. In your translation, express this in the way that a speaker of your language would politely disagree with someone. Alternate translation: [I do not think you need to speak that way]

10.q: וּ⁠מֶ֣לֶךְ יִשְׂרָאֵ֡ל וִֽ⁠יהוֹשָׁפָ֣ט מֶֽלֶךְ־יְהוּדָ֡ה יֹשְׁבִים֩ אִ֨ישׁ עַל־כִּסְא֜⁠וֹ מְלֻבָּשִׁ֤ים בְּגָדִים֙
10.note: The author is providing background information to help readers understand what happens next in the story. Micaiah demonstrated courage and faithfulness to Yahweh by speaking a difficult message truthfully despite the intimidating appearance of these kings. In your translation, introduce this information in a way that would be natural in your own language and culture.

The author is using **a man on his throne** as a common expression of his culture to mean “each on his own throne.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [each on his own throne]

The author says **all the prophets** as a generalization for emphasis. He may not mean that all 400 of Ahab’s prophets were present at this location. He may mean that many of them were present and were prophesying. If it would be clearer in your language, you could express the emphasis in a different way. Alternate translation: [And all the prophets who were there]

Here, **to their faces** represents being in the presence of these kings. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [in their presence]

11.q: כֹּֽה־אָמַ֣ר יְהוָ֔ה בְּ⁠אֵ֛לֶּה תְּנַגַּ֥ח אֶת־אֲרָ֖ם עַד־כַּלֹּתָֽ⁠ם
11.note: If it would be clearer in your language, you could translate this so that there is not a quotation within a quotation. Alternate translation: [Yahweh says that with these you will gore Aram until their finishing]

Now that Ahab’s prophets know that Jehoshaphat wants to hear a message from Yahweh, they are using his name rather than a title. Here and in the next verse, show that the prophets are using the name of Yahweh by representing it in the way that you have decided to do that regularly in your translation.

Zedekiah is speaking as if Ahab’s army were actually an ox with iron horns that could gore its enemies. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [You will defeat Aram completely, as if you had been an ox goring them with horns like these]

12.q: עֲלֵ֞ה רָמֹ֤ת גִּלְעָד֙ וְ⁠הַצְלַ֔ח וְ⁠נָתַ֥ן יְהוָ֖ה בְּ⁠יַ֥ד הַ⁠מֶּֽלֶךְ
12.note: If it would be more natural in your language, you could reverse the order of these phrases, since the second phrase gives the reason for the result that the first phrase describes. Alternate translation: [Since Yahweh will give it into the hand of the king, go up to Ramoth Gilead and prosper]

This is an imperative, but it describes a result rather than giving a command. Use a form in your language that describes a result, here and in verse 15. Alternate translation: [and you will prosper] or [and you will succeed]

13.note: See how you translated the similar expression in 1:14. Alternate translation: [Listen]

13.q: נָ֞א דִּבְרֵ֧י הַ⁠נְּבִיאִ֛ים & דברי⁠ך כִּ⁠דְבַ֛ר אַחַ֥ד מֵ⁠הֶ֖ם
13.note: The messenger is using the term **word** to represent what the prophets have been saying and what he hopes Micaiah will say by using words. If it would be clearer in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the things the prophets are saying … what you say … what one of them is saying]

The messenger is using the term **mouth** to represent speaking. He is using the idea of all the prophets using **one mouth** to speak to mean that they are saying the same thing. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [unanimously]

14.note: Following the custom of his culture, Micaiah is swearing an oath and guaranteeing it by something that he holds sacred. Use a natural way in your language to express an oath. Alternate translation: [I swear by Yahweh]

15.q: עֲלֵ֣ה וְ⁠הַצְלַ֔ח וְ⁠נָתַ֥ן יְהוָ֖ה בְּ⁠יַ֥ד הַ⁠מֶּֽלֶךְ
15.note: Micaiah actually means to communicate the opposite of the literal meaning of what he is saying here. (This is indicated by the way that he is imitating exactly what the other prophets have been saying.) If a speaker of your language would not say the opposite of what he meant, you could indicate what Micaiah is doing. Alternate translation: [I was told to say the same thing as the other prophets, so go up and prosper, for Yahweh will give it into the hand of the king]

16.q: עַד־כַּ⁠מֶּ֥ה פְעָמִ֖ים אֲנִ֣י מַשְׁבִּעֶ֑⁠ךָ אֲ֠שֶׁר לֹֽא־תְדַבֵּ֥ר אֵלַ֛⁠י רַק־אֱמֶ֖ת בְּ⁠שֵׁ֥ם יְהוָֽה
16.note: King Ahab is using the question form for emphasis. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [I have made you swear many times before that you would not speak about me except truth in the name of Yahweh!]

If it would appear in your language that the king was making a statement and then contradicting it, you could reword this as a positive statement. Alternate translation: [you would only speak truth about me]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **truth**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [things that are true]

Here, **the name of Yahweh** represents the authority of Yahweh. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [when speaking with Yahweh’s authority] or [when speaking on behalf of Yahweh]

17.note: Here, **Israel** represents the Israelite army. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [the whole Israelite army]

17.q: וַ⁠יֹּ֤אמֶר יְהוָה֙ לֹֽא־אֲדֹנִ֣ים לָ⁠אֵ֔לֶּה יָשׁ֥וּבוּ אִישׁ־לְ⁠בֵית֖⁠וֹ בְּ⁠שָׁלֽוֹם
17.note: If it would be clearer in your language, you could translate this so that there is not a quotation within a quotation. Alternate translation: [And Yahweh said that no masters were to these, so they should return, a man to his house, in peace]
See how you translated the similar expression in 12:24. Alternate translation: [Let each of them leave the army and return to his home]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **peace**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [peacefully]

18.q: הֲ⁠לוֹא֙ אָמַ֣רְתִּי אֵלֶ֔י⁠ךָ לֽוֹא־יִתְנַבֵּ֥א עָלַ֛⁠י ט֖וֹב כִּ֥י אִם־רָֽע
18.note: If it would be clearer in your language, you could translate this so that there is not a quotation within a quotation. Alternate translation: [Did I not tell you that he would not prophesy good about me, but rather evil]

18.q: הֲ⁠לוֹא֙ אָמַ֣רְתִּי אֵלֶ֔י⁠ךָ לֽוֹא־יִתְנַבֵּ֥א עָלַ֛⁠י ט֖וֹב כִּ֥י אִם־רָֽע
18.note: Ahab is using the question form to remind Jehoshaphat of what he had already told him and to emphasize that he was right. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [I told you that he would not prophesy good about me but rather evil!]
If your language does not use abstract nouns for the ideas of **good** and **evil**, you could express the same ideas in other ways. Alternate translation: [good things … bad things]

The author is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [but rather he will prophesy evil about me]

19.note: Here the word **Therefore** introduces not a reason but an explanation. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a different connecting word or phrase. Alternate translation: [Since you have asked me to speak only truth in the name of Yahweh]
Here, **word** represents what Yahweh said by using words. If it would be clearer in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [what Yahweh has said]

Micaiah is speaking of heavenly beings as if they were an **army**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and all of the heavenly beings were standing]

The author is using the adjectives **right** and **left** as nouns to mean certain sides. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate these adjectives with equivalent phrases. Alternate translation: [on his right side and on his left side]

20.q: וַ⁠יֹּ֣אמֶר יְהוָ֗ה מִ֤י יְפַתֶּה֙ אֶת־אַחְאָ֔ב וְ⁠יַ֕עַל וְ⁠יִפֹּ֖ל בְּ⁠רָמֹ֣ת גִּלְעָ֑ד וַ⁠יֹּ֤אמֶר זֶה֙ בְּ⁠כֹ֔ה וְ⁠זֶ֥ה אֹמֵ֖ר בְּ⁠כֹֽה
20.note: If it would be clearer in your language, you could translate this so that there is not a quotation within a quotation. Alternate translation: [And Yahweh asked who would deceive Ahab so that he would go up and fall at Ramoth Gilead. And one angel suggested one thing while another angel was suggesting something else]
Here, **fall** represents “die.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [and die]

21.note: Here, **to the face of** represents being in front of Yahweh. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [in front of Yahweh]
See how you translated the similar expression in 1:17. Alternate translation: [And he said, ‘I will be the one who deceives him]
If it would be clearer in your language, you could translate this so that there is not a quotation within a quotation. Alternate translation: [And he said that he would be the one who deceived him]

Yahweh is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [And Yahweh said to him, ‘By what means will you deceive him]
If it would be clearer in your language, you could translate this so that there is not a quotation within a quotation. Alternate translation: [And Yahweh asked him by what means he would deceive him]

22.q: וַ⁠יֹּ֗אמֶר אֵצֵא֙ וְ⁠הָיִ֨יתִי֙ ר֣וּחַ שֶׁ֔קֶר בְּ⁠פִ֖י כָּל־נְבִיאָ֑י⁠ו וַ⁠יֹּ֗אמֶר תְּפַתֶּה֙ וְ⁠גַם־תּוּכָ֔ל צֵ֖א וַ⁠עֲשֵׂה־כֵֽן
22.note: If it would be clearer in your language, you could translate this so that there are not quotations within quotations. Alternate translation: [And the spirit said that he would go out and be a spirit of falsehood in the mouth of all of Ahab’s prophets. And Yahweh told him that he would be able to deceive Ahab, so he should go out and do what he had suggested]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **falsehood**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [a lying spirit]

Here, **mouth** represents what the prophets would say. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [to influence what all of his prophets say]

The verbs **deceive** and **be able** express a single idea. If it would be more natural in your language, you could express this meaning in a different way. Alternate translation: [You will be able to deceive him]

23.note: **And now** was an expression that speakers in this culture commonly used to introduce their main topic. See how you have been translating it in contexts such as 1:12 and 2:16.

24.note: Striking someone **on the cheek** was a symbolic action by which Zedekiah showed contempt for Micaiah and his prophetic message. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could explain the significance of this action in the text of your translation or in a footnote. Alternate translation: [and struck Micaiah on the cheek to show contempt for him and what he had said] or [and slapped Micaiah on the cheek as an insult]

24.q: אֵי־זֶ֨ה עָבַ֧ר רֽוּחַ־יְהוָ֛ה מֵ⁠אִתִּ֖⁠י לְ⁠דַבֵּ֥ר אוֹתָֽ⁠ךְ
24.note: Zedekiah is using the question form for emphasis and to express his indignation. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [How dare you claim that the Spirit of Yahweh has passed over from with me to speak to you!]

25.note: See how you translated the similar expression in 11:22. Alternate translation: [You are about to see,]
See how you translated the similar expression in 20:30. Alternate translation: [an inner room] or [a private room]

26.note: The implied “you” in the imperative **Take** is singular because Ahab is speaking to the messenger who brought Micaiah to him. So use the singular form in your translation if your language marks that distinction.

Even though the king is referring to his own son, he is speaking of him in the third person as **the son of the king** because he is making a formal announcement. If it would be helpful in your language, you could translate this in the first person. Alternate translation: [my son]

27.q: וְ⁠אָמַרְתָּ֗ כֹּ֚ה אָמַ֣ר הַ⁠מֶּ֔לֶךְ שִׂ֥ימוּ אֶת־זֶ֖ה בֵּ֣ית הַ⁠כֶּ֑לֶא וְ⁠הַאֲכִילֻ֨⁠הוּ לֶ֤חֶם לַ֨חַץ֙ וּ⁠מַ֣יִם לַ֔חַץ עַ֖ד בֹּאִ֥⁠י בְ⁠שָׁלֽוֹם
27.note: There are three levels of quotation here. The author is quoting what Ahab told his officials (level 1), continuing from the previous verse. Ahab tells his officials what to say to Amon and Joash (level 2). That includes a direct quotation from Ahab himself (level 3). Use the appropriate punctuation in your language to mark these levels of quotation. Alternatively, you could translate this so that there are not second-level or third-level quotations (see the Quotes within Quotes note).

27.q: וְ⁠אָמַרְתָּ֗ כֹּ֚ה אָמַ֣ר הַ⁠מֶּ֔לֶךְ שִׂ֥ימוּ אֶת־זֶ֖ה בֵּ֣ית הַ⁠כֶּ֑לֶא וְ⁠הַאֲכִילֻ֨⁠הוּ לֶ֤חֶם לַ֨חַץ֙ וּ⁠מַ֣יִם לַ֔חַץ עַ֖ד בֹּאִ֥⁠י בְ⁠שָׁלֽוֹם
27.note: If it would be clearer in your language, you could translate this so that there is not a quotation within a quotation. Alternate translation: [And you shall tell them that I say that they are to put this one in the house of imprisonment and feed him bread of affliction and water of affliction until my coming in peace]

The implied “you” in the imperatives **Put** and **feed** is plural because the messengers would be addressing Amon and Joash, so use the plural form in your translation if your language marks that distinction.
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **imprisonment**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the prison building]

The king is using **bread of affliction and water of affliction** as a common expression of his culture to mean the scanty food and drink that people would have during a time of **affliction**, such as during a siege. If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [scanty food and drink]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **peace**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [peacefully]

28.note: Micaiah is repeating forms of the verb **return** in order to intensify his expression of the idea that it conveys. If your language can repeat words for intensification, it would be appropriate to do that here in your translation. If not, your language may have another way of expressing the intensification. Alternate translation: [you indeed return]

By **peoples**, Micaiah means the tribes of Israel, and he is using **them** to represent the Israelites from various tribes who were present in Samaria to hear his prophecy. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [you tribes of Israel, all of you] or [you Israelites, all of you]
Since Micaiah is referring to people who are present, it may be more natural in your language to use a second-person pronoun here. Alternate translation: [all of you]

30.note: In a context such as this, your language might say “went” instead of **came**. Alternate translation: [and go into the battle … and he went into the battle]
See how you translated the similar expression in 12:4. Alternate translation: [but for your part, wear your robes]

31.q: לֹ֚א תִּלָּ֣חֲמ֔וּ אֶת־קָטֹ֖ן וְ⁠אֶת־גָּד֑וֹל כִּ֛י אִֽם־אֶת־מֶ֥לֶךְ יִשְׂרָאֵ֖ל לְ⁠בַדּֽ⁠וֹ
31.note: The king of Aram is referring to all the soldiers his troops might encounter by naming two extremes, **small** and **great**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [You shall not fight with anyone except with the king of Israel alone]

31.q: לֹ֚א תִּלָּ֣חֲמ֔וּ אֶת־קָטֹ֖ן וְ⁠אֶת־גָּד֑וֹל כִּ֛י אִֽם־אֶת־מֶ֥לֶךְ יִשְׂרָאֵ֖ל לְ⁠בַדּֽ⁠וֹ
31.note: If it would appear in your language that the king of Aram was making a statement and then contradicting it, you could reword this as a positive statement. Alternate translation: [You shall only fight with the king of Israel himself, not with anyone else]

32.note: The author is stating the pronoun **they** separately, even though the verb translated as **they said** already includes this meaning. He is doing that to indicate that this action took place at the same time as when they **saw Jehoshaphat**. If a speaker of your language would use an explicit pronoun for the same purpose, you may want to use that construction in your translation. If not, your language may have other ways of showing the meaning here. Alternate translation: [that right away they said]

34.note: The author is using **drew with the bow** as a common expression of his culture to mean “shot an arrow.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [shot an arrow]

The author is using **in his innocence** as a common expression of his culture to mean “without knowing at whom he was shooting” or “without aiming intentionally.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [at random] or [without aiming]

The terms **joints** and **armor** together express a single idea. If it would be more natural in your language, you could express this meaning in a different way. Alternate translation: [between the joints of his armor]

34.q: הֲפֹ֥ךְ יָדְ⁠ךָ֛ וְ⁠הוֹצִיאֵ֥⁠נִי מִן־הַֽ⁠מַּחֲנֶ֖ה כִּ֥י הָחֳלֵֽיתִי
34.note: If it would be more natural in your language, you could reverse the order of these phrases, since the second phrase gives the reason for the result that the first phrase describes. Alternate translation: [I am wounded, so turn your hand and bring me out from the camp]

Here, **hand** represents the driver’s direction or control of the chariot. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Turn the chariot around]

Here, **the camp** represents the soldiers who would stay in a **camp** near a battlefield. Ahab wants his driver to bring him out from the midst of the army, but the context makes clear that he wants to stay on the battlefield, though at a safe distance from the fighting. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [from the ranks] or [from the midst of our soldiers]

35.note: The author is saying **the battle went up** as a common expression of his culture to mean that the fighting became more intense or severe. If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And the tide of battle rose higher] or [And the fighting became fiercer]

35.q: וְ⁠הַ⁠מֶּ֗לֶךְ הָיָ֧ה מָעֳמָ֛ד בַּ⁠מֶּרְכָּבָ֖ה נֹ֣כַח אֲרָ֑ם
35.note: Being **propped up in the chariot** facing the enemy army was a symbolic action by which Ahab wanted to depict that he was still in command of his army despite being wounded. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could explain the significance of this action in the text of your translation or in a footnote. Alternate translation: [and the king was propped up in the chariot opposite Aram so that he would still appear to be in command]

The expression **was propped up** is a passive verbal form. If your language would not use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [and the king’s soldiers propped him up]

35.q: וַ⁠יָּ֣מָת בָּ⁠עֶ֔רֶב וַ⁠יִּ֥צֶק דַּֽם־הַ⁠מַּכָּ֖ה אֶל־חֵ֥יק הָ⁠רָֽכֶב
35.note: The author is describing one event before describing another event that preceded it. If it would be helpful in your language, you may wish to relate these events in the order in which they happened. Alternate translation: [And the blood of the wound poured out onto the bosom of the chariot, and he died in the evening]

The author is using the term **bosom** to mean the interior of Ahab’s **chariot**. If this term does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the interior of the chariot]

36.note: The author is speaking of this **cry** as if it were a living thing that could have **passed through** the Israelite **camp**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And throughout the camp one soldier shouted to another]

The author is using **the going of the sun** as a common expression of his culture to mean “at sunset.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [at sunset] or [at sundown]

These two phrases **A man to his city** and **a man to his land** mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could connect the phrases in a way that shows that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. Alternate translation: [A man to his city, yes, a man to his land]

The phrase **A man to his city, and a man to his land** was a common expression meaning “Let each soldier leave the army and return to his home.” When the Israelite soldiers said this, it was a fulfillment of what Micaiah predicted in 22:17. See how you translated the similar expression there. Alternate translation: [Let each of us leave the army and return to his home]

37.note: The implication is that Ahab’s soldiers brought his body back to Samaria. You could indicate this in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [and his soldiers brought his body back to Samaria]

The author is using the pronoun **they** in a general sense, not to refer to specific people. Use an expression for this that would be natural in your language. Alternate translation: [And the Israelites buried the king] or [And the king was buried]

38.q: וַ⁠יִּשְׁטֹ֨ף אֶת־הָ⁠רֶ֜כֶב עַ֣ל ׀ בְּרֵכַ֣ת שֹׁמְר֗וֹן וַ⁠יָּלֹ֤קּוּ הַ⁠כְּלָבִים֙ אֶת־דָּמ֔⁠וֹ וְ⁠הַ⁠זֹּנ֖וֹת רָחָ֑צוּ
38.note: If it would be more natural in your language, you may want to put the information that **the prostitutes bathed there** with the information that Ahab’s chariot was washed at **the pool of Samaria**. Alternate translation: [And one washed the chariot at the pool of Samaria (now the prostitutes bathed there). And dogs licked up his blood]

The author is using the pronoun **one** in a general sense, not to refer to a specific person. Use an expression for this that would be natural in your language. Alternate translation: [And the chariot was washed]

The author is providing background information to help readers understand the nature of the location where these events took place. Together with the information that dogs licked up Ahab’s blood, this information associates the death of Ahab, who was once a proud king, with shameful circumstances. In your translation, introduce this information in a way that would be natural in your own language and culture.

Here, the term **word** represents what Yahweh said by using words. If it would be clearer in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [according to what Yahweh said when he spoke through Micaiah]

39.q: וְ⁠יֶתֶר֩ דִּבְרֵ֨י אַחְאָ֜ב וְ⁠כָל־אֲשֶׁ֣ר עָשָׂ֗ה וּ⁠בֵ֤ית הַ⁠שֵּׁן֙ אֲשֶׁ֣ר בָּנָ֔ה וְ⁠כָל־הֶ⁠עָרִ֖ים אֲשֶׁ֣ר בָּנָ֑ה הֲ⁠לֽוֹא־הֵ֣ם כְּתוּבִ֗ים עַל־סֵ֛פֶר דִּבְרֵ֥י הַ⁠יָּמִ֖ים לְ⁠מַלְכֵ֥י יִשְׂרָאֵֽל
39.note: In this verse and the next verse, the author is using phrases that he regularly uses to conclude accounts of kings’ reigns. See how you translated the similar phrases in 11:41–43 and other comparable contexts in the book. Alternate translation: [Now you can read about the rest of the matters of Ahab and all that he did and the house of ivory that he built and all of the cities that he built in the book of the matters of the days of the kings of Israel]

40.note: See how you translated the similar expression in 1:21. Alternate translation: [And Ahab passed away]

41.q: וִ⁠יהֽוֹשָׁפָט֙ בֶּן־אָסָ֔א מָלַ֖ךְ עַל־יְהוּדָ֑ה בִּ⁠שְׁנַ֣ת אַרְבַּ֔ע לְ⁠אַחְאָ֖ב מֶ֥לֶךְ יִשְׂרָאֵֽל
41.note: In this verse, the author is introducing **Jehoshaphat** as a participant in the story as the new king of **Judah**. See how you translated the similar phrases in [15:1–2](ta:15) and other comparable contexts in the book.

If your language would not represent a number in a form such as **four** in a context like this one, you could represent this number in a form that your language would use. Alternate translation: [in the fourth year]

42.note: See how you translated the similar expression in 14:21. Alternate translation: [was 35 years old]

43.q: וַ⁠יֵּ֗לֶךְ בְּ⁠כָל־דֶּ֛רֶךְ אָסָ֥א אָבִ֖י⁠ו לֹא־סָ֣ר מִמֶּ֑⁠נּוּ
43.note: See how you translated the similar expression in 15:26. Alternate translation: [And he lived just as Asa his father had lived, without ever ceasing to live that way]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **right**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [what was right]
See how you translated the similar expression in 3:10. Alternate translation: [in the judgment of Yahweh]

The author is using the pronoun **they** in a general sense, not to refer to specific people. Use an expression for this that would be natural in your language. Alternate translation: [no one removed the high places] or [the high places were not removed]

44.note: If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **peace**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [established peaceful relations]

45.q: וְ⁠יֶ֨תֶר דִּבְרֵ֧י יְהוֹשָׁפָ֛ט וּ⁠גְבוּרָת֥⁠וֹ אֲשֶׁר־עָשָׂ֖ה וַ⁠אֲשֶׁ֣ר נִלְחָ֑ם הֲ⁠לֹֽא־הֵ֣ם כְּתוּבִ֗ים עַל־סֵ֛פֶר דִּבְרֵ֥י הַ⁠יָּמִ֖ים לְ⁠מַלְכֵ֥י יְהוּדָֽה
45.note: In this verse and in verse 50, the author is using phrases that he regularly uses to conclude accounts of kings’ reigns. See how you translated the similar phrases in 11:41–43 and other comparable contexts in the book. Alternate translation: [Now you can read about the rest of the matters of Jehoshaphat and his mighty things that he did and how he fought in the book of the matters of the days of the kings of Judah]

46.note: The expression **were left** is a passive verbal form. If your language would not use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [whom Asa his father left in his days]
The author is using the term **days** to refer to a specific time period. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [during the reign of]

The author is speaking of removing the cultic prostitutes as if Jehoshaphat had actually **burned** them. He means that Jehoshaphat completely removed them from the land. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [he completely removed from the land]

48.note: See how you translated the similar expression in 10:22. Alternate translation: [a fleet of long-range ships]

48.q: וְ⁠לֹ֣א הָלָ֑ךְ כִּֽי־נשברה אֳנִיּ֖וֹת בְּ⁠עֶצְי֥וֹן גָּֽבֶר
48.note: If it would be more natural in your language, you could reverse the order of these phrases, since the second phrase gives the reason for the result that the first phrase describes. Alternate translation: [but because the ships were broken at Ezion Geber, he did not go]

The author is using one person who was involved in this action, Jehoshaphat, referring to him as **he**, to represent everyone who was involved. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression from your culture or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [but they never set sail]

The expression **were broken** is a passive verbal form. If your language would not use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [because a storm broke up the ships]

50.note: See how you translated the similar expression in 1:21. Alternate translation: [And Jehoshaphat passed away]

The expression **he was buried** is a passive verbal form. If your language would not use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [and people buried him]
See how you translated the similar expression in 1:21. Alternate translation: [with his ancestors … his ancestor]

51.q: אֲחַזְיָ֣הוּ בֶן־אַחְאָ֗ב מָלַ֤ךְ עַל־יִשְׂרָאֵל֙ בְּ⁠שֹׁ֣מְר֔וֹן בִּ⁠שְׁנַת֙ שְׁבַ֣ע עֶשְׂרֵ֔ה לִ⁠יהוֹשָׁפָ֖ט מֶ֣לֶךְ יְהוּדָ֑ה
51.note: In this verse, the author is introducing **Ahaziah** as a participant in the story as the new king of **Israel**. See how you translated the similar phrases in [15:1–2](ta:15) and other comparable contexts in the book.

If your language would not represent a number in a form such as **17** in a context like this one, you could represent this number in a form that your language would use. Alternate translation: [in the seventeenth year]

52.note: If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **evil**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [what was evil]
See how you translated the similar expression in 3:10. Alternate translation: [in the judgment of Yahweh]

52.q: וַ⁠יֵּ֗לֶךְ בְּ⁠דֶ֤רֶךְ אָבִי⁠ו֙ וּ⁠בְ⁠דֶ֣רֶךְ אִמּ֔⁠וֹ וּ⁠בְ⁠דֶ֨רֶךְ֙ יָרָבְעָ֣ם בֶּן־נְבָ֔ט אֲשֶׁ֥ר הֶחֱטִ֖יא אֶת־יִשְׂרָאֵֽל
52.note: See how you translated the similar expression in 15:26. Alternate translation: [And he lived as his father and his mother had lived and as Jeroboam, the son of Nebat, had lived, who had led the Israelites to sin]
